title: When should you use WebSocket vs SSE — WebSocket for chat, gaming, collaborative editing (need two-way); SSE for live notifications, stock tickers, dashboards (server→client only, simpler, auto-reconnect)?
shortTitle: When should you use WebSocket vs SSE

s1_definition.profdef: WebSocket and Server-Sent Events are both persistent-connection techniques for real-time updates, but they differ in directionality and complexity. WebSocket provides full-duplex, two-way communication over a single upgraded TCP connection, suited to interactive scenarios like chat, gaming, and collaborative editing. SSE provides one-way server-to-client streaming over a single long-lived HTTP connection with built-in automatic reconnection, suited to server-push-only scenarios like live notifications, stock tickers, and dashboards. You choose by whether the client needs to send data back in real time and by how much complexity you want.
s1_definition.analogy: At National Bank of India, picture two situations. In the first, a trader and the market-data desk must talk back and forth continuously — the trader shouts orders, the desk shouts confirmations — so they need an open two-way phone line, which is WebSocket. In the second, the bank just broadcasts the live share price over a loudspeaker to everyone watching their dashboard — the bank talks, the customers only listen, and if a customer steps out and comes back the loudspeaker is still playing — that is SSE. If all you need is to broadcast, the one-way loudspeaker is simpler and self-healing; only when both sides must speak do you set up the two-way line.
s1_definition.oneliner: Use WebSocket when the client must send data back in real time (chat, gaming, trading, collaboration); use SSE when the server only pushes to the client (notifications, tickers, dashboards), because SSE is simpler and auto-reconnects.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** WebSocket and Server-Sent Events are both persistent-connection techniques for real-time updates, but they differ in directionality and complexity. WebSocket provides full-duplex, two-way communication over a single upgraded TCP connection, suited to interactive scenarios like chat, gaming, and collaborative editing. SSE provides one-way server-to-client streaming over a single long-lived HTTP connection with built-in automatic reconnection, suited to server-push-only scenarios like live notifications, stock tickers, and dashboards. You choose by whether the client needs to send data back in real time and by how much complexity you want.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At National Bank of India, picture two situations. In the first, a trader and the market-data desk must talk back and forth continuously — the trader shouts orders, the desk shouts confirmations — so they need an open two-way phone line, which is WebSocket. In the second, the bank just broadcasts the live share price over a loudspeaker to everyone watching their dashboard — the bank talks, the customers only listen, and if a customer steps out and comes back the loudspeaker is still playing — that is SSE. If all you need is to broadcast, the one-way loudspeaker is simpler and self-healing; only when both sides must speak do you set up the two-way line.

**One line to remember:** Use WebSocket when the client must send data back in real time (chat, gaming, trading, collaboration); use SSE when the server only pushes to the client (notifications, tickers, dashboards), because SSE is simpler and auto-reconnects.

sections.s3_banking:
At National Bank of India two real-time features sit side by side, and choosing correctly keeps the system simple.

Problem 1 — customers want live payment and fraud-alert notifications pushed to their app the instant they happen. This is purely server-to-client; the app only listens. Using WebSocket here would mean building reconnection and heartbeats for a one-way feed, so SSE is the right choice, with its automatic reconnection and HTTP friendliness.

Problem 2 — the live stock ticker on the dashboard streams prices to thousands of watchers. Again this is one-way broadcast, so SSE fits, and HTTP/2 multiplexing handles many connections.

Problem 3 — the active trading terminal needs the trader to send orders and receive fills interactively with minimal latency, and the two directions are independent and concurrent. This genuinely needs two-way messaging, so WebSocket is correct.

Problem 4 — the notification feature occasionally needs the client to acknowledge an alert. Rather than complicate the SSE stream, the acknowledgment is a simple REST POST alongside the one-way stream, which keeps SSE clean.

The code will contain: an SSE notification controller, an SSE price ticker, a WebSocket trading handler, a REST acknowledgment endpoint beside the SSE stream, and a demo showing each feature using the right technique.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: Rajesh runs the banking app with live notifications and a price ticker, and separately opens the trading terminal.

Step 1 — SSE notifications. Rajesh's app opens one SSE connection to the notifications endpoint. The server stores his emitter and keeps the connection open. The app only listens; it sends nothing on this channel. When a fraud alert fires, the fraud service calls push, and the server writes an event down the open connection, which the app renders instantly.

Step 2 — reconnection. Rajesh's phone briefly loses signal and the SSE connection drops. The browser's EventSource automatically reconnects and, using the last event id, the server can resume from where it left off. Rajesh did not miss an alert, and no reconnection code was written by hand. This self-healing is a key reason SSE fits one-way feeds.

Step 3 — SSE ticker. Rajesh's dashboard opens a second SSE stream for the RELIANCE price. The server pushes a new price every second. Thousands of other watchers have their own one-way streams, and HTTP/2 multiplexing keeps this manageable. Again the client only listens.

Step 4 — client action beside SSE. Rajesh taps to acknowledge the fraud alert. Rather than complicating the one-way SSE channel, the app sends a plain REST POST to the ack endpoint. The SSE stream stays purely server-to-client and simple.

Step 5 — WebSocket trading. Rajesh opens the trading terminal, which upgrades to a WebSocket. Now he sends an order and receives a fill on the same open connection, both directions flowing independently and with low latency. This two-way interaction is precisely why trading uses WebSocket while notifications and the ticker use SSE.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 02:10:13 INFO NotificationController - SSE notification stream opened for rajesh
2026-10-26 02:10:15 INFO AckController - User rajesh acknowledged alert ALERT-9
2026-10-26 02:10:17 INFO TradingHandler - Order in: {"symbol":"RELIANCE","qty":100}
```

```

              (drop? → EventSource auto-reconnects, resume via Last-Event-ID)
   occasional action: Rajesh ─POST /ack─→ server   (separate REST, keeps SSE simple)

  WEBSOCKET (trading) — TWO WAY
   Rajesh terminal ─HTTP Upgrade→101─ server
   Rajesh ── order ──→ server
   Rajesh ←── fill ──── server     (both send freely, one connection)

  Decision:
   server→client only  → SSE  (simpler, auto-reconnect, HTTP-friendly)
   real-time two-way   → WebSocket
```

  5. trading → WS handleTextMessage(order) → sendMessage(fill)

sections.s6_takeaway:
WebSocket and Server-Sent Events are both persistent-connection real-time techniques, but they differ in direction and complexity. WebSocket is full-duplex: after an HTTP upgrade handshake, both client and server can send messages at any time over one connection, which suits genuinely interactive two-way scenarios like chat, multiplayer gaming, collaborative editing, and a trading terminal. SSE is one-way: the server streams events to the client over a single long-lived HTTP connection, and the client cannot send on that channel, which suits server-push-only scenarios like live notifications, stock tickers, and dashboards.

I default to SSE whenever the requirement is purely server-to-client, because it is simpler and more robust for that job. It runs over plain HTTP, so it passes through proxies and firewalls that sometimes block WebSocket upgrades and it reuses my existing HTTP auth, and the browser's EventSource reconnects automatically and can resume from the last event id, which I would otherwise have to build myself. I reach for WebSocket only when real-time client-to-server messaging is genuinely needed, accepting that I then own reconnection, heartbeats, and WebSocket-aware infrastructure, and lose HTTP caching.

At National Bank of India this kept the system clean. Live payment and fraud-alert notifications and the stock-price ticker are purely one-way, so they run on SSE, with automatic reconnection meaning a customer who briefly loses signal does not miss an alert. The active trading terminal, where the trader sends orders and receives fills interactively at low latency, genuinely needs two-way messaging, so it uses WebSocket. And when the notification feature needed the client to acknowledge an alert, I did not complicate the SSE stream; the acknowledgment is a plain REST POST alongside the one-way stream.

The mistake I consciously avoid is reaching for WebSocket reflexively for every real-time feature and then carrying its extra complexity for a feed that only ever pushes one way. The decision rule is simple: if the client must push in real time, use WebSocket; otherwise use SSE, and if a mostly-one-way feature needs an occasional client action, make that action an ordinary REST call so the streaming channel stays simple. Matching the channel to the actual direction of the data is what keeps a bank's real-time features both responsive and maintainable at scale.
